meta.headline: Thames Water rescue deal should be rejected - MPs

relevance.reason: A regulated water monopoly, fines, creditors and the case for temporary nationalisation link directly to market power, regulation and government intervention.

mapping.justification: The central issue is whether the government should intervene, through special administration (a form of temporary nationalisation), in a regulated water company that is heavily in debt and is being fined for poor performance.
mapping.cross_theme_note: The article also links to Theme 1 (government failure, negative externalities from pollution) and Theme 4 (public sector finances, because the government could take on liabilities).

paragraphs: A cross-party committee of MPs has urged the government to reject a £10bn takeover proposal from Thames Water's creditors. Thames Water, the UK's biggest water company, serves 16 million customers and owes roughly £20bn.

The Environment, Food and Rural Affairs Committee said the government should consider placing the company into special administration, a form of temporary nationalisation. It said the creditors' plan, backed by more than 100 lenders who hold about £17bn of the debt, does not have the interests of the public, the company or the environment at heart, and that the bidders' priority is to extract value rather than secure long-term success.

The report says Thames Water and other poor-performing water companies are in a doom loop: fines for poor performance leave them with less money to invest in improvements. It warned that Thames Water would likely face more than £900m of penalties over the next five years. The committee wants the law changed so that the government can trigger special administration on performance grounds alone.

The committee's chair said Thames Water can be turned around, and that the government's short-term liabilities could be recovered by selling the company once its finances and performance are back on track. Thames Water says it needs to be recapitalised and that delays risk slowing its turnaround. The bidders, London & Valley Water, say they have never controlled the company or received a dividend, and that their improved proposal addresses feedback from the regulator Ofwat and ministers.

Water is an essential service that most customers cannot buy from anyone else, so the company's behaviour is controlled by regulators and, if it fails, by the government. This article shows the difficult choices when a regulated monopoly is heavily in debt: leave it to private creditors, keep fining it, or take it under temporary public control.

concepts: Natural monopoly and regulation of monopoly power
Government intervention: fines, regulation and nationalisation
Government failure and the cost of intervention
Debt, creditors and the risk of business failure
chain: Water is close to a natural monopoly: Thames Water serves 16 million customers who cannot switch supplier, and duplicate pipes would raise costs, so it has to be regulated and can be fined for poor performance.

The fines cut the money available for investment, so performance stays poor and more fines follow (MPs call this a doom loop, with more than £900m of penalties expected over five years). This shows a limit to regulation: a regulator can punish a firm with no rival but cannot make it invest.
The company owes about £20bn, and its creditors' £10bn takeover plan is criticised by MPs for putting extracting value ahead of long-term success, which is a profit motive with weak accountability.
MPs urge the government to consider special administration, a form of temporary nationalisation, so that the government, not shareholders, sets the aim of the business (service and the environment).

The impact could be better quality and environmental outcomes for customers, but efficiency may fall without a profit motive and the government takes on short-term liabilities that taxpayers may bear.
The MPs' chair says costs could be recovered by selling the company once its finances and performance are back on track, but this depends on that recovery happening.

evaluation.label: Regulation
evaluation.text: fines are meant to improve performance, but the article says they can leave companies with less to invest, so the tool may sometimes make the problem worse.

evaluation.label: Short run and long run
evaluation.text: the government would face liabilities immediately, but the committee says these could be recovered by a later sale.

evaluation.label: Who is affected
evaluation.text: 16 million customers, creditors who hold about £17bn of the debt, taxpayers and the environment all have different interests.

evaluation.label: Incentives
evaluation.text: MPs say the bidders want to extract value, while London & Valley Water says it has never received a dividend and that its plan addresses regulators' feedback, so the evidence is disputed.

evaluation.label: Law and time
evaluation.text: the committee says the law must change to allow special administration on performance alone, so the option may not be quick.

key_terms.definition: A market where one firm can supply the whole market at a lower average cost than several firms, often because of very high fixed costs such as a pipe network.
Rules and oversight set by the government or a regulator, such as Ofwat, to control the behaviour of firms.
The regulator of the water industry in England and Wales.
The transfer of a private sector firm into public ownership and control.
A process, described in the article as a form of temporary nationalisation, in which the government takes control of a failing water company to keep services running.
A person or organisation that is owed money, such as a lender.
Putting new money or restructuring debt to give a firm a stronger financial position.
A cost imposed on third parties that is not paid by the producer, such as pollution from a firm.

questions.prompt: Thames Water owes roughly £20bn, and its creditors own about £17bn of that debt. Approximately what percentage of its debt do the creditors own?
Why can most Thames Water customers not switch to a rival water supplier?

options.text: Water supply is a perfectly competitive market
Water supply is a natural monopoly because duplicating the pipe network would be very costly
Customers are not allowed to change suppliers by tax law

questions.explanation: Building competing pipe networks would be very expensive, so one regulated firm usually supplies each area.

questions.prompt: How does the article describe special administration?

options.text: A permanent sale to private investors
A new type of fine for pollution

questions.explanation: The article describes it as a form of temporary nationalisation, where the government takes control of the company.

questions.prompt: Explain one reason why the government might place Thames Water into special administration.

points: Identifies a valid reason, such as protecting an essential service, protecting consumers or the environment, or preventing a disorderly collapse of a monopoly supplier.
Uses the article, for example 16 million customers, debt of about £20bn, the doom loop of fines, or MPs saying the creditors' plan does not have the public's interests at heart.

Develops a chain, for example: temporary public control would keep services running and protect customers from the effects of financial failure (1), and would allow spending on investment to continue instead of being cut by fines and debt repayments, improving performance and reducing pollution (1).

notes: Award 1 mark for a partial chain and 2 for a complete one.

questions.prompt: Assess whether the government should place Thames Water into special administration.

points: Natural monopoly and the need for regulation.
Government intervention through regulation, fines and nationalisation.
Government failure.
Externalities from pollution.
16 million customers.
Debt of about £20bn.
Creditors holding about £17bn and offering a £10bn takeover.
More than £900m of likely penalties over five years.
The doom loop of fines.
MPs' view that the bidders want to extract value.
Thames Water's view that it needs recapitalisation.

For special administration: it keeps services running, could put customers and the environment ahead of creditors, could break the doom loop by allowing investment, and costs could be recovered by a later sale. Analysis against: the government would face short-term liabilities and risk, the law would need to change, public ownership may not solve poor performance and creditors may challenge it.
Judge using the size of the liabilities compared with the benefits, how long the process would take, whether the creditors' plan could be improved instead, and the effect on different groups.
A supported conclusion should weigh short-term costs against the long-term aim of a stable, well-run water supply.
